youtube.description:
Bleeding gums when you brush are common, and most often caused by plaque build-up that leads to gingivitis. In this video we explain why it happens and what simple daily habits can help.

This video is for general education only and is not a substitute for professional advice. If bleeding continues for more than two weeks, book a check-up with your dentist.

style.broll: None. The sheets show a single source frame for the full 84 s, with no cut-aways, inserts, diagrams or zooms. The content (plaque, gingivitis, brushing at 45 degrees) would suit B-roll or diagrams, but the reference doesn't use any.
style.hook: The video opens with a generic greeting ("Hi everyone, welcome back to the clinic channel") and then states the topic ("why your gums bleed when you brush") after a flubbed first attempt. There is no cold open, teaser or title card. The topic and promise (what to do about it) come within the first ~10 s.
style.pacing: There are zero cuts (average shot 84 s), so all pacing comes from the speaker's delivery: about 116 wpm, speech present 53% of the time, and roughly 11 pauses over 0.6 s per minute with an average gap of 1.38 s. This is a slow, breathing rhythm. The reference leaves flubs, restarts ("sorry, let me start that again", "Wait, I forgot what comes next. Hold on") and fillers ("um, so") in place. To match the pacing on new footage, keep one continuous shot and the relaxed pauses between sentences. Trim the dead-air and flub sections, since the reference's own 1.38 s average gap is longer than a tight edit needs.
rules: Keep the main talking-head angle as one continuous shot with no hard cuts and no more than 1 cut per minute.
Do not add B-roll, stock cut-aways or zooms; the speaker stays on screen throughout.
Leave natural breathing room between sentences, around 1.0-1.4 s on average, rather than tight jump-cut spacing.
Allow about 10-12 pauses longer than 0.6 s per minute so delivery stays near 115 words per minute.
Do not speed up the footage or compress the delivery; leave speech at natural speed.
Open straight on the greeting and topic statement with no cold open, intro animation or music sting; state the topic within about 10 s.
Do not add captions, lower thirds or graphics unless the new brief asks for them.
Remove retakes and dead-air flubs where the footage allows (for example 'sorry, let me start that again'); the reference keeps them, so only keep them if a raw, unpolished feel is wanted.
Close on a plain verbal call to action ('subscribe, see you in the next video') with no end card.
Keep the framing static and unchanged for the whole video.
style.summary: A plain, unbroken single-camera talking-head explainer: one continuous 84 s shot with no cuts, graphics or B-roll. The contact sheets show only a placeholder card (blue gradient labelled "TALKING HEAD (source)" with a timecode), so framing and on-screen visuals could not be judged. The style judged from the transcript and measurements is calm, educational and unhurried. The raw take is conversational, with a restart, a mid-sentence stumble and filler words that a tighter edit would remove.

styles.description: Tight jump cuts, retakes removed, B-roll every ~12 s
styles.instructions:
- Open with the strongest, most specific line as a hook (first 5–10 s). Move it to the front only if it works out of context.
- Remove every retake and false start; keep the last complete take unless an earlier one is clearly better.
- Remove meta talk ("let me start again", "is this recording?"), dead air, filler-only bits and repeated points.
- Keep the speaker's personality: a short laugh or aside that adds warmth can stay.
- B-roll over long explanations, lists and anything the speaker describes visually. Never cover the hook or the call to action.
- On-screen titles only for key terms, numbers and section changes. Keep them under 6 words.
- End on the call to action; cut anything after it.
styles.name: Talking-head YouTube

styles.description: Clear, accurate patient education with safe visuals
styles.instructions:
- Accuracy first: never cut a sentence in a way that changes medical meaning, drops a caveat, or removes "consult your dentist/doctor" advice.
- Hook with the patient's problem or question (e.g. "Why do your gums bleed when you brush?").
- Remove retakes, stumbles, meta talk and dead air. Keep a calm, trustworthy pace – not hyper-fast.
- Use titles for key terms, numbers and steps (e.g. "2 minutes, twice a day").
- B-roll must be generic and non-graphic: toothbrushes, floss, a smiling patient, a clean clinic, a calendar. No surgery, blood, needles or anatomy close-ups. No brand names.
- Add chapters for each question or step.
- In notes, flag any statement that sounds medically questionable so a professional can check it.
styles.name: Doctor / dentist explainer

styles.description: Natural pauses, atmosphere and story kept
styles.instructions:
- Tell a story with a beginning, middle and end. Keep moments that show emotion or atmosphere.
- Cut boring logistics, repeated takes and long silences, but keep natural breathing room.
- Use the B-roll library generously for scene-setting and transitions between locations.
- Titles for places, times and chapters of the day.
styles.name: Vlog / day in the life

styles.description: Under 60 s, hook in 2 s, very tight, vertical
styles.instructions:
- The whole edit must be under 60 seconds. Pick the single best idea and drop everything else.
- The first 2 seconds must hook: a bold claim, a question or a surprising fact.
- Cut every pause, breath and filler. No intros like "hi guys" or "welcome back".
- Callout titles for the key words (2–4 words each). End with a quick call to action or a loop back to the hook.
styles.name: Shorts / Reels

styles.description: Every step kept and labelled, few distractions
styles.instructions:
- Never remove a step. Remove mistakes only when a corrected version exists.
- Title each step ("Step 1 – …") and add a chapter for each.
- Cut waiting time and silence, but keep pauses where the viewer needs to follow an action.
- B-roll only when it clarifies something; the main footage is usually the point.
styles.name: Tutorial / how-to

styles.instructions:
- Keep questions and answers complete; never splice half-answers together.
- Remove crosstalk, false starts, technical interruptions and long silences.
- Lower thirds for each speaker's name the first time they speak (if known from the brief).
- Chapters for each topic.
styles.name: Podcast / interview clip
